content: 1. The case fatality rate for patients with inhalation anthrax who were treated in intensive care units was 45%, as observed in 5 out of 11 cases. 2. Systemic anthrax can lead to massive septicemia, with bacterial counts reaching 10^7 to 10^8 organisms per milliliter of blood, accompanied by toxemia. This condition rapidly progresses to systemic effects such as high fever and shock, often resulting in death within a short period. 3. Studies using laboratory animals and nonhuman primates have shown hematogenous dissemination of Bacillus anthracis to abdominal organs and the central nervous system. This is associated with systemic inflammation, increased vascular permeability, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. 4. Autopsy findings from the 1979 Sverdlovsk anthrax outbreak and the 2001 bioterrorism events revealed hepatic congestion, congestive necrosis of the spleen, and submucosal gastrointestinal lesions. 5. Anthrax meningitis has been reported in all three clinical forms of anthrax (cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and inhalation). It likely results from hematogenous spread across the blood-brain barrier and typically presents as hemorrhagic meningitis. 6. Anthrax meningitis is characterized by a fulminant and rapidly progressive clinical course. Despite aggressive therapeutic interventions, the condition is usually fatal. 7. Patients with severe systemic Bacillus anthracis infections have a high likelihood of developing clinical or subclinical meningitis. 8. A review of 82 cases of inhalation anthrax from 1900 to 2005 revealed 70 fatal cases. Among the 70 fatalities, 11 of 61 patients with available data exhibited signs of meningeal involvement, whereas none of the 12 survivors showed such signs. Additionally, 44 of the 70 deceased patients developed meningoencephalitis during their illness, compared to none of the survivors. 9. Nonhuman primate studies have demonstrated meningeal involvement in 33% to 77% of experimental inhalation anthrax cases. 10. Human anthrax is best controlled through preventive measures, including pre-exposure vaccination for individuals at high risk of encountering aerosolized Bacillus anthracis spores, vaccination of livestock in endemic areas, and environmental controls to reduce exposure to contaminated animal products such as imported hides and skins. 11. Post-exposure prophylaxis combining antimicrobial therapy and vaccination provides the best available protection for individuals exposed to aerosolized Bacillus anthracis spores. 12. The incidence of naturally occurring human anthrax in the United States has been significantly reduced through livestock vaccination, improved industrial hygiene, and decreased use of contaminated imported raw materials. 13. Effective animal disease control programs have reduced the global incidence of animal anthrax and, consequently, human anthrax. 14. Since the initiation of annual livestock vaccination in endemic regions in 1957, the number of naturally occurring human anthrax cases in the United States has decreased from 38 cases in 1956 to fewer than two cases annually between 1980 and 2008. 15. Anthrax in livestock can be controlled through vaccination programs, rapid detection and reporting of cases, and proper disposal of carcasses of animals suspected or confirmed to have anthrax, preferably by incineration. 16. In regions where anthrax is common and livestock vaccination coverage is low, humans should avoid contact with livestock and animal products that have not been inspected and certified as healthy before and after slaughter. 17. Consumption of meat from animals that died suddenly and without explanation, or meat of uncertain origin, should be avoided. 18. Methods for sterilizing or inactivating Bacillus anthracis spores on contaminated materials include steam sterilization, ethylene oxide gas sterilization, boiling, dry heat, or treatment with formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, or hypochlorite for specified durations and concentrations. Air drying does not destroy Bacillus anthracis spores. 19. Industrial exposure to Bacillus anthracis has been controlled through improved hygiene standards, mechanization of animal processing, and strict importation guidelines. However, the risk to employees working with animals and animal products has not been completely eliminated. 20. Published precautions for minimizing exposure when handling potentially contaminated animal hides should be followed. 21. The first effective anthrax vaccines, developed in the 1880s by William S. Greenfield and Louis Pasteur, used live, attenuated Bacillus anthracis cultures. 22. Pasteur's vaccine involved a two-step inoculation process: a primary inoculation with Bacillus anthracis incubated at 42–43°C for 15–20 days (type I vaccine), followed by a secondary inoculation with a less attenuated strain incubated at 42–43°C for 10–12 days (type II vaccine). 23. This duplex vaccine was widely used until approximately 1935, when the procedure was modified to exclude the type I vaccine and reduce the virulence of the type II vaccine by adding 1%–10% saponin. 24. In 1939, Max Sterne developed a live, attenuated spore vaccine from an avirulent, non-capsulated variant of Bacillus anthracis. 25. Sterne-type vaccines replaced Pasteur's heat-attenuated formulations as the veterinary vaccines of choice. 26. The veterinary vaccine currently used in the United States is based on the Bacillus anthracis Sterne 34F2 strain and is produced using a deep culture technique, yielding approximately 10^5 doses per liter. 27. A single dose of this vaccine provides effective immunity in animals for at least one year, with revaccination recommended to maintain protection beyond one year. 28. The feasibility of using acellular vaccines against Bacillus anthracis is under investigation.
